sentences.text: Around 400 million people now live in countries which have legalised assisted dying.
sentences.article_title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world

sentences.text: Canada, Australia, New Zealand, Spain and Austria have all introduced assisted dying laws since 2015 – when UK MPs last voted on the issue – some allowing assisted death for those who are not terminally ill.
sentences.article_title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world

sentences.text: Just last month, France adopted an 'aid in dying' law for adults with incurable conditions causing them unbearable pain.
sentences.article_title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world

sentences.text: While most jurisdictions forbid medical help to die, assisted dying laws around the world vary.
sentences.article_title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world

sentences.text: Across the US, assisted dying - which some critics prefer to call assisted suicide - is legal in 30 out of 50 states, as well as in Washington DC.
sentences.article_title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world

sentences.text: Oregon was one of the first places in the world to offer help to die for some patients, in 1997, and so has nearly 30 years' experience.
sentences.article_title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world

sentences.text: It has become the model on which other US assisted dying laws have been framed.
sentences.article_title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world

sentences.text: In Oregon, assisted dying is open to terminally ill , external , mentally competent adults expected to die within six months - and must be signed off by two doctors.
sentences.article_title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world

sentences.text: Since 1997 , external , 5,520 people have received a prescription for a lethal dose of medication - with 3,691 deaths.
sentences.article_title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world

sentences.text: In a 2025 report , external , 61% of patients who ask for help to die had cancer, 14% had a neurological condition like motor neurone disease and 11% had heart disease.
sentences.article_title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world

sentences.text: Around one in three of those prescribed a lethal dose don’t go ahead with it.
sentences.article_title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world

sentences.text: Oregon is important for supporters of assisted dying in England and Wales as they point out it has remained restricted to terminally ill adults since its introduction.
sentences.article_title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world

sentences.text: However, opponents say some of the rules have been relaxed.
sentences.article_title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world

sentences.text: A residency requirement has been lifted, which means it is open to people from outside the state.
sentences.article_title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world

sentences.text: The number of assisted deaths has also risen substantially over the years.
sentences.article_title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world

sentences.text: Canada is the country often cited by opponents of assisted dying as an example of the so-called "slippery slope" - a place where assisted dying has been extended and made available to more people since it was first brought in.
sentences.article_title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world

sentences.text: Medical assistance in dying (Maid) , external was introduced in 2016, initially just for the terminally ill.
sentences.article_title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world

sentences.text: This was amended in 2021 and extended to those experiencing "unbearable suffering" from an irreversible illness or disability.
sentences.article_title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world

sentences.text: It had been due to be extended to people with a mental illness but that is now on hold.
sentences.article_title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world

sentences.text: Critics say the more the law is widened, the more disabled and vulnerable people will be put at risk.
sentences.article_title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world

sentences.text: There has also been a dramatic growth in the number of people using Maid.
sentences.article_title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world

sentences.text: Roughly one in every 20 deaths in Canada are now medically assisted , external , compared to about one in 100 in Oregon.
sentences.article_title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world

sentences.text: Across Europe, six countries have some form of legalised assisted dying: Switzerland, the Netherlands, Belgium, Luxembourg, Spain, Austria and - most recently - France.
sentences.article_title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world

sentences.text: In all of them - unlike the proposals in England and Wales - help to die is not restricted to the terminally ill.
sentences.article_title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world

sentences.text: Switzerland was the first country in the world to create a “right to die” when it made assisted suicide legal in 1942.
sentences.article_title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world

sentences.text: It is one of the few countries which allows foreigners access to help to die via organisations like Dignitas, in Zurich.
sentences.article_title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world

sentences.text: More than 600 Britons have died at Dignitas , external in the past two decades, including 43 last year.
sentences.article_title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world

sentences.text: The lethal medication must be self-administered.
sentences.article_title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world

sentences.text: The Netherlands and Belgium both legalised assisted dying more than 20 years ago for patients experiencing unbearable suffering from an incurable illness, including mental health issues.
sentences.article_title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world

sentences.text: It has since been extended to children - the only European countries to allow this.
sentences.article_title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world

sentences.text: Both allow euthanasia - or physician-assisted dying.
sentences.article_title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world

sentences.text: Most recently, Spain and Austria have legalised assisted dying for both terminal illness and intolerable suffering.
sentences.article_title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world

sentences.text: In Austria, the drugs must be self-administered, whereas in Spain a medical professional can administer them.
sentences.article_title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world

sentences.text: In England, Wales and Scotland, parliament has so far rejected assisted dying proposals.
sentences.article_title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world

sentences.text: But assisted dying has already been legalised in one part of the British Isles.
sentences.article_title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world

sentences.text: In July, Royal Assent was given to a bill in Jersey.
sentences.article_title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world

sentences.text: Unlike at Westminster and Holyrood, the legislation was introduced by the Jersey government, which says it will take about 18 months to set up the service.
sentences.article_title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world

sentences.text: The first assisted death could happen late next year.
sentences.article_title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world

sentences.text: There will be a residency requirement of one year, in a bid to prevent so-called 'death tourism'.
sentences.article_title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world

sentences.text: The measure, which most sets apart the Jersey legislation from the rest of the British Isles, concerns the manner in which those eligible for an assisted death can end their lives.
sentences.article_title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world

sentences.text: Individuals will be able to choose to have a doctor administer a lethal dose intravenously, as happens in Spain, Canada, New Zealand and most of Australia.
sentences.article_title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world

sentences.text: This is, in effect, voluntary euthanasia.
sentences.article_title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world

sentences.text: It has become the preferred method of assisted dying in jurisdictions which allow this choice.
sentences.article_title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world

sentences.text: The laws proposed at Westminster, Holyrood and Tynwald - Isle of Man - all state that death must be by self-administration, which usually means the individual swallowing a lethal dose.
sentences.article_title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world

sentences.text: The Isle of Man assisted dying bill was passed by Tynwald (the Manx parliament) in March last year.
sentences.article_title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world

sentences.text: As a UK Crown Dependency - like Jersey - it could not become law until granted Royal Assent.
sentences.article_title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world

sentences.text: This was declined earlier this year by the UK Ministry of Justice, but Tynwald has since passed an updated bill which has been sent back to the UK government for a second time.
sentences.article_title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world

sentences.text: If Royal Assent is granted, the Isle of Man expects the service to be operational next year.
sentences.article_title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world

sentences.text: There is a residency requirement of five years.
sentences.article_title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world

sentences.text: In the past few years voluntary assisted dying has become legal across most of Australia.
sentences.article_title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world

sentences.text: Last month, the Northern Territory parliament became the last part of Australia to pass Voluntary Assisted Dying legislation.
sentences.article_title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world

sentences.text: In New Zealand, patients must be terminally ill and expected to die within six months.
sentences.article_title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world

sentences.text: That is extended to 12 months for those with a neurodegenerative condition in much of Australia.
sentences.article_title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world

sentences.text: In both countries, patients can self-administer the lethal medication.
sentences.article_title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world

sentences.text: But it can also be administered by a doctor or nurse, usually via an intravenous injection.
sentences.article_title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world

sentences.text: The UK needs new regulations for AI products used in the NHS and other healthcare settings, says Britain's industry watchdog.

sentences.text: The Medicines and Healthcare Products Regulatory Agency (MHRA), which regulates all medical devices and licenses treatment drugs in the UK, has published 44 recommendations to update its policies as the use of AI in the sector rises.
sentences.article_title: UK needs new laws for AI in healthcare, says watchdog

sentences.text: The technology will soon be routinely used within the NHS, MHRA chief Lawrence Tallon told the BBC.
sentences.article_title: UK needs new laws for AI in healthcare, says watchdog

sentences.text: "What I would expect is that patients will... increasingly see AI as part of the way that normal NHS healthcare is delivered," he said.
sentences.article_title: UK needs new laws for AI in healthcare, says watchdog

sentences.text: "That should happen in a way that they can maintain their trust and their confidence in what's happening." The report was compiled by an independent commission and involved input from more than 12,000 people including patients and clinicians.
sentences.article_title: UK needs new laws for AI in healthcare, says watchdog

sentences.text: He added while current guidelines may work for simple AI products trained to spot known symptoms on scans, for example, the rules do not apply to more complex models.
sentences.article_title: UK needs new laws for AI in healthcare, says watchdog

sentences.text: "Unlike most of the medical products we're used to regulating, these products continue to change after the point of authorization," he said.
sentences.article_title: UK needs new laws for AI in healthcare, says watchdog

sentences.text: "As new data gets fed in, they learn, they adapt, they drift." And he acknowledged trying to regulate AI is a global challenge.
sentences.article_title: UK needs new laws for AI in healthcare, says watchdog

sentences.text: "I don't think at this moment in time we can point to a single country, a single regulatory framework, and say that they have absolutely cracked it," he said.

sentences.text: Regularly drinking beverages like tea and coffee at very hot temperatures increases the risk of cancer of the food pipe or gullet, known as oesophageal cancer, UK research suggests.
sentences.article_title: Very hot drinks may damage the food pipe and increase cancer risk

sentences.text: Researchers say the findings , external , from a study of nearly a million people, make this the largest to date to establish the link.
sentences.article_title: Very hot drinks may damage the food pipe and increase cancer risk

sentences.text: In the study, people who had their drinks "very hot" had around a three times higher risk of the cancer than "warm" tea or coffee drinkers - although experts stress the overall chances of developing this cancer are low.
sentences.article_title: Very hot drinks may damage the food pipe and increase cancer risk

sentences.text: Steaming hot liquid can damage the cell lining of the food pipe on the way down to the stomach.
sentences.article_title: Very hot drinks may damage the food pipe and increase cancer risk

sentences.text: The work by Oxford University, which is published in the International Journal of Cancer, defines any drink at 65 degrees Celsuis or above as "very hot" and posing a potential risk.
sentences.article_title: Very hot drinks may damage the food pipe and increase cancer risk

sentences.text: Consuming six or more hot drinks per day also raises the risk, according to data from 977,282 middle-aged men and women.
sentences.article_title: Very hot drinks may damage the food pipe and increase cancer risk

sentences.text: Although adding milk can cool drinks down slightly, a milky tea or coffee may still be far too hot, researchers say.
sentences.article_title: Very hot drinks may damage the food pipe and increase cancer risk

sentences.text: Tea made immediately after a kettle is fully boiled is touching boiling point, which is 100 degrees C (212 degrees F).
sentences.article_title: Very hot drinks may damage the food pipe and increase cancer risk

sentences.text: Once poured into a cup, that lowers to around 90 or 95 degrees C.
sentences.article_title: Very hot drinks may damage the food pipe and increase cancer risk

sentences.text: The advice is to wait a few minutes before drinking so the beverage cools to a safer temperature.
sentences.article_title: Very hot drinks may damage the food pipe and increase cancer risk

sentences.text: Cancer Research UK says it's difficult to put an exact time on how long a hot drink should be left to cool.
sentences.article_title: Very hot drinks may damage the food pipe and increase cancer risk

sentences.text: "But if you're worried, we'd suggest just waiting until it's comfortable to drink rather than drinking it while it's still very hot," the charity said.
sentences.article_title: Very hot drinks may damage the food pipe and increase cancer risk

sentences.text: Lead researcher Dr Keren Papier said research in South America - where many people drink a very hot herbal beverage called mate - had already shown a similar link between hot drinks and oesophageal cancer.
sentences.article_title: Very hot drinks may damage the food pipe and increase cancer risk

sentences.text: But she said: "More research is now needed to identify the exact drink temperatures linked to this increased risk." A separate study , external of 118 young adults who did multiple tastings of different black coffees found most only deemed the drinks to be too hot if the temperature was 70 degrees C or above.
sentences.article_title: Very hot drinks may damage the food pipe and increase cancer risk

sentences.text: According to one takeaway coffee cup manufacturer, the ideal temperature for hot coffee on the go is between 49 and 60 degrees C.
sentences.article_title: Very hot drinks may damage the food pipe and increase cancer risk

sentences.text: Should a barista want the coffee to stay hotter for longer - if a customer requests extra hot - it can be served at over 82 degrees C, says MTPak Coffee.
sentences.article_title: Very hot drinks may damage the food pipe and increase cancer risk

sentences.text: The researchers suggest that around one or two in every 10 oesophageal cancers could be avoided if people stopped drinking very hot beverages.
sentences.article_title: Very hot drinks may damage the food pipe and increase cancer risk

sentences.text: Squamous cell oesophageal cancer is rare, affecting a few thousand people a year.
sentences.article_title: Very hot drinks may damage the food pipe and increase cancer risk

sentences.text: In the UK, around 1% of the population has a lifetime risk of being diagnosed with this type of cancer.
sentences.article_title: Very hot drinks may damage the food pipe and increase cancer risk

sentences.text: So even if scalding hot drinks might increase someone's risk, the chances of them developing the cancer are still low.
sentences.article_title: Very hot drinks may damage the food pipe and increase cancer risk

sentences.text: And there are other factors, such as smoking, which are a bigger risk for oesophageal cancer.
sentences.article_title: Very hot drinks may damage the food pipe and increase cancer risk

sentences.text: Fiona Osgun from Cancer Research UK, which funded the study, stressed: "The most important ways to reduce the risk of this cancer type are not smoking and cutting down on alcohol." Symptoms of oesophageal cancer can include heartburn, indigestion or a pain in your throat or chest, along with weight loss.

sentences.text: Protesters demonstrating against benefit cuts at a rally in Parliament Square in 2025 Support for disability benefits remains "remarkably strong" and cutting them would be "politically risky" according to a new report.
sentences.article_title: Support for disability benefits 'remarkably strong' report finds

sentences.text: The analysis, from the British Social Attitudes survey, found that fewer than one in 10 people favoured cutting welfare payments for the disabled, with almost half of people saying they would support more being spent on them, even if it led to higher taxes.
sentences.article_title: Support for disability benefits 'remarkably strong' report finds

sentences.text: The report comes amid mounting concerns among several political parties about the growing cost of disability benefits.
sentences.article_title: Support for disability benefits 'remarkably strong' report finds

sentences.text: Spending on the main disability benefit is forecast to more than double in a decade, reaching £41bn by 2030.
sentences.article_title: Support for disability benefits 'remarkably strong' report finds

sentences.text: But the report says that cutting these payments would not be easy.
sentences.article_title: Support for disability benefits 'remarkably strong' report finds

sentences.text: "Despite growing political divisions on welfare, support for disability benefits remains remarkably strong," said Dr Robert de Vries from the University of Kent, who was one of the report's co-authors.
sentences.article_title: Support for disability benefits 'remarkably strong' report finds

sentences.text: "Very few people favour cuts, disabled people are seen as among the most deserving recipients of support, and proposals to reduce disability benefits appear politically risky across the political spectrum." The analysis is based on 4,656 interviews gathered between August and October 2025.
sentences.article_title: Support for disability benefits 'remarkably strong' report finds

sentences.text: The authors noted that the timing of the interviews, just after the Sir Keir Starmer's government had failed to reform PIP, meant it was "possible that people were particularly supportive of disability benefits at the time".
sentences.article_title: Support for disability benefits 'remarkably strong' report finds

sentences.text: They cautioned that public attitudes to disability benefits "crucially depend on which disabled people are in the public's mind", referencing previous research that showed that "some types of disabled people are seen as 'deserving' by the public".
sentences.article_title: Support for disability benefits 'remarkably strong' report finds

sentences.text: The findings come despite the proportion of those who support increasing welfare spending for the poor being at a near record low.
sentences.article_title: Support for disability benefits 'remarkably strong' report finds

sentences.text: Labour, the Conservative party and Reform UK have all said there is a need to reduce the amount of money being spent on health and disability benefits, while the Liberal Democrats, Greens and SNP oppose reductions.
sentences.article_title: Support for disability benefits 'remarkably strong' report finds

sentences.text: Efforts by Sir Keir to introduce cuts last year were opposed by many in his own party, forcing a government climbdown .
sentences.article_title: Support for disability benefits 'remarkably strong' report finds

sentences.text: The proportion of GDP the UK spends on all welfare benefits for those of working age has remained broadly flat over the past 40 years, at just under 5%.
sentences.article_title: Support for disability benefits 'remarkably strong' report finds

sentences.text: It has occasionally increased to over 5%, including in the 1990s, after the financial crisis in 2008, and during the Covid pandemic.
sentences.article_title: Support for disability benefits 'remarkably strong' report finds

sentences.text: Despite that, the survey found that support for increasing welfare payments to help the poor was close to the lowest level the researchers have ever recorded.
sentences.article_title: Support for disability benefits 'remarkably strong' report finds

sentences.text: Asked if "the government should spend more money on welfare benefits for the poor, even if it leads to higher taxes," 27% replied they should while 42% were opposed.
sentences.article_title: Support for disability benefits 'remarkably strong' report finds

sentences.text: While wider welfare spending on people of working age has, proportionately, remained stable, payments for disability benefits have taken up an increasing share of the total.
sentences.article_title: Support for disability benefits 'remarkably strong' report finds

sentences.text: The latest figures show four million people in England and Wales are currently in receipt of Personal Independence Payment (PIP), the main disability benefit.
sentences.article_title: Support for disability benefits 'remarkably strong' report finds

sentences.text: Annual spending has increased sharply from £16.3bn in 2019/20 to £27.3bn in 2024/25, and is forecast to rise to more than £41bn by 2030.
sentences.article_title: Support for disability benefits 'remarkably strong' report finds

sentences.text: But around half of those polled for the survey, 49%, supported higher spending on disability benefits overall even if it led to higher taxes.
sentences.article_title: Support for disability benefits 'remarkably strong' report finds

sentences.text: Just 7% were in favour of cutting such benefits for disabled people who cannot work.
sentences.article_title: Support for disability benefits 'remarkably strong' report finds

sentences.text: A majority also strongly backed extra payments for the costs of having a disability.
sentences.article_title: Support for disability benefits 'remarkably strong' report finds

sentences.text: Around 83% of respondents supported additional payments to help with cooking, 80% for budgeting, and 78% for washing.
sentences.article_title: Support for disability benefits 'remarkably strong' report finds

sentences.text: Just 3% replied that "nobody should get any additional money" for all three tasks.
sentences.article_title: Support for disability benefits 'remarkably strong' report finds

sentences.text: Respondents were not asked if they thought it should be harder to claim those benefits.
sentences.article_title: Support for disability benefits 'remarkably strong' report finds

sentences.text: Proposals to reform PIP are due to be unveiled by the government in the autumn after an interim report published in the summer found the benefit was not fit for purpose .
sentences.article_title: Support for disability benefits 'remarkably strong' report finds

sentences.text: Around 57% of Labour voters polled for the survey favoured more spending on disability benefits.
sentences.article_title: Support for disability benefits 'remarkably strong' report finds

sentences.text: But there was broad political consensus that cuts would be wrong – just 5% of Labour voters, 7% of Conservatives and 11% of Reform UK backers said they supported cuts to those payments.

sentences.text: Have you ever slept next to a snoring partner and woken up feeling stressed, unfocused or forgetful the next day?
sentences.article_title: 'Like a hangover': Why your partner's snoring could be impacting your health

sentences.text: As snoring is relatively common, it is often left untreated and dismissed as a harmless irritation.
sentences.article_title: 'Like a hangover': Why your partner's snoring could be impacting your health

sentences.text: But according to experts, sleeping next to a snorer could be impacting your health.
sentences.article_title: 'Like a hangover': Why your partner's snoring could be impacting your health

sentences.text: Snoring is caused by the vibration of the soft tissues in our upper airways during sleep, explains Dr Clare Simon, a dentist with a special interest in dental sleep medicine.
sentences.article_title: 'Like a hangover': Why your partner's snoring could be impacting your health

sentences.text: About 40% of the UK adult population snores, with the issue affecting more men than women, says the British Snoring and Sleep Apnoea Association (BSSAA).
sentences.article_title: 'Like a hangover': Why your partner's snoring could be impacting your health

sentences.text: And 75% of people with a snoring partner say they have had their sleep impacted, according to a US survey by the Sleep Foundation.
sentences.article_title: 'Like a hangover': Why your partner's snoring could be impacting your health

sentences.text: Here's what you need to know about the impact on partners - and what you can do about it.
sentences.article_title: 'Like a hangover': Why your partner's snoring could be impacting your health

sentences.text: Prof Ama Johal, a consultant orthodontist and sleep expert at Aerox Health, explains that the partner of a snorer can become "so impacted upon that it's almost a last-ditch effort on their part to get up and go sleep in a separate room because they have to sleep".
sentences.article_title: 'Like a hangover': Why your partner's snoring could be impacting your health

sentences.text: He adds: "As humans we physically can't function without that necessity." Prof Ama Johal says many couples put up with the negative effects snoring for too long During the night, we cycle through different stages of sleep in repeating patterns, usually every 90 minutes.
sentences.article_title: 'Like a hangover': Why your partner's snoring could be impacting your health

sentences.text: The deeper stages of this cycle are important for physical restoration.
sentences.article_title: 'Like a hangover': Why your partner's snoring could be impacting your health

sentences.text: If sleep is frequently disrupted, you may spend less time in the restorative stages, meaning you can wake up feeling tired, even if you've spent a lot of time in bed, the BSSAA explains.
sentences.article_title: 'Like a hangover': Why your partner's snoring could be impacting your health

sentences.text: Your brain processes and stores information from the day during sleep.
sentences.article_title: 'Like a hangover': Why your partner's snoring could be impacting your health

sentences.text: Fragmented sleep - which can happen if you're waking up due to a snoring partner - can interrupt this process, impacting your focus and memory.
sentences.article_title: 'Like a hangover': Why your partner's snoring could be impacting your health

sentences.text: Disrupted sleep can also impact hormone regulation, which affects your energy levels and motivation.
sentences.article_title: 'Like a hangover': Why your partner's snoring could be impacting your health

sentences.text: Sleep also plays a role in regulating the brain systems involved in stress and emotional response.
sentences.article_title: 'Like a hangover': Why your partner's snoring could be impacting your health

sentences.text: When it is disrupted, these systems can become less balanced, which may make you feel more irritable and less able to cope with stress.
sentences.article_title: 'Like a hangover': Why your partner's snoring could be impacting your health

sentences.text: This is something Meg Warren, 29, experienced when her former partner's snoring would keep her up.
sentences.article_title: 'Like a hangover': Why your partner's snoring could be impacting your health

sentences.text: She says: "Without fail, after a snoring-induced wake up I would feel on incredibly high alert." Meg, a charity media officer, would prod him throughout the night and try to coax him from his back to his side.
sentences.article_title: 'Like a hangover': Why your partner's snoring could be impacting your health

sentences.text: She says she would wake up "feeling groggy and dazed, sometimes so much so that it would feel like a hangover".
sentences.article_title: 'Like a hangover': Why your partner's snoring could be impacting your health

sentences.text: Meg Warren felt 'groggy and dazed' after a night of little sleep due to her former partner's snoring Anna-Louise Dearden, a 52-year-old journalist, says she sometimes sleeps in a separate room from her partner due to his snoring.
sentences.article_title: 'Like a hangover': Why your partner's snoring could be impacting your health

sentences.text: Having this option allows her to prioritise getting enough rest when the snoring is particularly bad.
sentences.article_title: 'Like a hangover': Why your partner's snoring could be impacting your health

sentences.text: There are things that can be done, say both Simon and Johal.
sentences.article_title: 'Like a hangover': Why your partner's snoring could be impacting your health

sentences.text: But first, it is important to distinguish whether your partner is simply snoring, or whether they have sleep apnoea.
sentences.article_title: 'Like a hangover': Why your partner's snoring could be impacting your health

sentences.text: "What you don't want to do is simply make someone quieter at night while potentially missing an underlying sleep-related breathing disorder," Simon says.
sentences.article_title: 'Like a hangover': Why your partner's snoring could be impacting your health

sentences.text: Signs of sleep apnoea, a disorder that causes a person's breathing to repeatedly stop and start during sleep, include pauses in breathing, choking at night, waking frequently, and suffering from morning headaches.
sentences.article_title: 'Like a hangover': Why your partner's snoring could be impacting your health

sentences.text: If this is what you are dealing with, you could be recommended a Continuous Positive Airway Pressure (CPAP) machine, or even surgical treatment in some cases, Simon explains.
sentences.article_title: 'Like a hangover': Why your partner's snoring could be impacting your health

sentences.text: For simple snoring, Simon said that lifestyle changes can make a difference, such as losing weight, stopping smoking, reducing alcohol intake before bed, or changing your sleeping position - such as laying on your side rather than your back.
sentences.article_title: 'Like a hangover': Why your partner's snoring could be impacting your health

sentences.text: You can also suggest to your partner that they see a GP, who will be able to advise further or refer you to a specialist.
sentences.article_title: 'Like a hangover': Why your partner's snoring could be impacting your health

sentences.text: An expert might suggest treating nasal obstruction or allergies, if this is what is causing snoring, or wearing a custom mouthguard to gently push the lower jaw forward and keep the airway open.
sentences.article_title: 'Like a hangover': Why your partner's snoring could be impacting your health

sentences.text: Sarah Mackay, known as @fitwsarah online, says her energy levels change through her cycle A woman points to a colour-coded grid dividing the menstrual cycle into four phases, each paired with a different list of exercises.
sentences.article_title: Menstrual fitness: Why some women are 'cycle-syncing' their workouts

sentences.text: "When you're bleeding, you want to be doing steady-pace jogging, Pilates, barre, walking, resting," she tells viewers.
sentences.article_title: Menstrual fitness: Why some women are 'cycle-syncing' their workouts

sentences.text: This is one of thousands of videos on TikTok and Instagram suggesting that people change their workouts depending on where they are in their menstrual cycles - something known as 'cycle-syncing'.
sentences.article_title: Menstrual fitness: Why some women are 'cycle-syncing' their workouts

sentences.text: So-called cycle-syncing workout plans have surged in popularity online, with Google searches for the term rising 740% since 2022 and more than 55,000 TikTok videos now using the #cyclesyncing hashtag.
sentences.article_title: Menstrual fitness: Why some women are 'cycle-syncing' their workouts

sentences.text: Most of the advice is shared by fitness and wellness creators rather than medical or research experts.
sentences.article_title: Menstrual fitness: Why some women are 'cycle-syncing' their workouts

sentences.text: Kelly McNulty, a researcher at Leeds Beckett University specialising in menstrual cycles and exercise, says there is evidence that some women experience changes in symptoms, energy or perceived strength across their cycle.
sentences.article_title: Menstrual fitness: Why some women are 'cycle-syncing' their workouts

sentences.text: But that is different from evidence that all women should train in a particular way at a particular point, she tells the BBC, adding that these videos are "a trend based on marketing rather than any kind of research or evidence".
sentences.article_title: Menstrual fitness: Why some women are 'cycle-syncing' their workouts

sentences.text: "There isn't any research to support that kind of phase-based prescription," she says.
sentences.article_title: Menstrual fitness: Why some women are 'cycle-syncing' their workouts

sentences.text: This video can not be played Should you sync your exercise routine with your period?
sentences.article_title: Menstrual fitness: Why some women are 'cycle-syncing' their workouts

sentences.text: A key issue is that menstrual cycles are highly individual, McNulty adds - they can differ between women, and one woman's experience can also change from one cycle to the next.
sentences.article_title: Menstrual fitness: Why some women are 'cycle-syncing' their workouts

sentences.text: That makes the blanket advice often found on social media difficult to apply, she explains.
sentences.article_title: Menstrual fitness: Why some women are 'cycle-syncing' their workouts

sentences.text: Many cycle-tracking apps and programmes are also designed around relatively regular menstrual cycles that are 21 to 35 days, which can make their recommendations less applicable to people with irregular periods, or those using hormonal contraception.
sentences.article_title: Menstrual fitness: Why some women are 'cycle-syncing' their workouts

sentences.text: She doesn't follow a prescriptive plan, she says, but instead makes changes intuitively.
sentences.article_title: Menstrual fitness: Why some women are 'cycle-syncing' their workouts

sentences.text: "In my luteal phase I'll try and ease off in the training," she tells the BBC.
sentences.article_title: Menstrual fitness: Why some women are 'cycle-syncing' their workouts

sentences.text: "In my follicular phase, I'm so energised, I feel like I can lift so much heavier.
sentences.article_title: Menstrual fitness: Why some women are 'cycle-syncing' their workouts

sentences.text: I like to try and get my long runs in." Burgoyne also welcomes the growing attention on women's health, and says that exercise and nutrition research has historically focused heavily on male bodies, with findings then often applied to women.
sentences.article_title: Menstrual fitness: Why some women are 'cycle-syncing' their workouts

sentences.text: Sarah says she has sometimes hit personal records while on her period Fitness creator Sarah Mackay, known as @liftwsarah on Instagram and TikTok, has also noticed her energy, motivation, cramps and mood change through the month.
sentences.article_title: Menstrual fitness: Why some women are 'cycle-syncing' their workouts

sentences.text: But she deliberately avoids strict plans because, she says, "there are too many variables at play".
sentences.article_title: Menstrual fitness: Why some women are 'cycle-syncing' their workouts

sentences.text: Some online plans advise women to avoid intense training during their period, she says, yet she has sometimes hit personal records while menstruating.
sentences.article_title: Menstrual fitness: Why some women are 'cycle-syncing' their workouts

sentences.text: "The problem is not that the menstrual cycle is irrelevant," she says, but that "not everything is predictable".
sentences.article_title: Menstrual fitness: Why some women are 'cycle-syncing' their workouts

sentences.text: Dr Faye Bate, a trained medical doctor and women's health expert, is also wary of advice suggesting all women should train differently according to their menstrual phase.
sentences.article_title: Menstrual fitness: Why some women are 'cycle-syncing' their workouts

sentences.text: "A one-size-fits-all model of 'you should be exercising this way in this phase and a different way in a different phase' shouldn't be advice that applies to all women," she says.
sentences.article_title: Menstrual fitness: Why some women are 'cycle-syncing' their workouts

sentences.text: She is concerned that repeatedly telling women they are likely to be weaker or less capable at particular points in their cycle could create a "nocebo" effect - where negative expectations themselves influence how someone feels or performs.
sentences.article_title: Menstrual fitness: Why some women are 'cycle-syncing' their workouts

sentences.text: McNulty tells the BBC that routinely easing off resistance training could also limit progress.
sentences.article_title: Menstrual fitness: Why some women are 'cycle-syncing' their workouts

sentences.text: Strength training is particularly important for women, who face a higher risk of osteoporosis later in life.
sentences.article_title: Menstrual fitness: Why some women are 'cycle-syncing' their workouts

sentences.text: While cycle-syncing itself may not be backed by strong evidence, the experts we spoke to did suggest being "cycle-aware".
sentences.article_title: Menstrual fitness: Why some women are 'cycle-syncing' their workouts

sentences.text: McNulty says tracking your cycle can be a useful way to understand your own patterns, while Dr Bate also encourages women to become more familiar with how they feel at different points in the month.
sentences.article_title: Menstrual fitness: Why some women are 'cycle-syncing' their workouts

sentences.text: Both welcome the fact that menstrual health is being discussed more openly, but say the focus should be on individual experience, rather than rigid, phase-based rules.
sentences.article_title: Menstrual fitness: Why some women are 'cycle-syncing' their workouts

sentences.text: In practice, that might mean having painkillers ready before your period, taking a rest day when symptoms are worse, or easing off a workout if you feel unusually fatigued.
sentences.article_title: Menstrual fitness: Why some women are 'cycle-syncing' their workouts

sentences.text: For Dr Bate, "the most important part is tuning in to how you feel".
sentences.article_title: Menstrual fitness: Why some women are 'cycle-syncing' their workouts

sentences.text: In other words, use your cycle as information rather than a set of rules.
sentences.article_title: Menstrual fitness: Why some women are 'cycle-syncing' their workouts

sentences.text: Take it too far, and you could end up with "orthosomnia" - the clinical term for an obsession with achieving perfect sleep.
sentences.article_title: Why 'sleepmaxxing' could be making your sleep worse

sentences.text: While it's not formally recognised as a condition in the UK, doctors tell the BBC they've noticed signs of orthosomnia in their patients, with some bringing their sleep tracker data into appointments convinced, wrongly, that they have a sleep disorder.
sentences.article_title: Why 'sleepmaxxing' could be making your sleep worse

sentences.text: That fixation is actually making people's sleep worse, they warn.
sentences.article_title: Why 'sleepmaxxing' could be making your sleep worse

sentences.text: So how and why did sleep become so complicated?
sentences.article_title: Why 'sleepmaxxing' could be making your sleep worse

sentences.text: And if sleepmaxxing isn't the answer, what is the elusive secret to a good night's sleep?
sentences.article_title: Why 'sleepmaxxing' could be making your sleep worse

sentences.text: The first commercial fitness tracker to incorporate sleep analysis was the Fitbit Classic in 2009.
sentences.article_title: Why 'sleepmaxxing' could be making your sleep worse

sentences.text: Since then, many others - including Garmin, Whoop and Apple - have integrated sleep trackers into wrist-worn devices, as have smart rings such as Oura, Ultrahuman and RingConn.
sentences.article_title: Why 'sleepmaxxing' could be making your sleep worse

sentences.text: These devices vary, but in general they all provide users with a report of their night, broken down by sleep stages - time awake, light sleep, deep sleep, and REM (rapid eye movement).
sentences.article_title: Why 'sleepmaxxing' could be making your sleep worse

sentences.text: Many also give users a "sleep score".
sentences.article_title: Why 'sleepmaxxing' could be making your sleep worse

sentences.text: But the concept of a sleep score is "completely made up", according to Dr Alanna Hare, consultant of sleep medicine at the Royal Brompton Hospital in London.
sentences.article_title: Why 'sleepmaxxing' could be making your sleep worse

sentences.text: "There's nothing recognised in sleep science that is a 'sleep score'," she tells the BBC.
sentences.article_title: Why 'sleepmaxxing' could be making your sleep worse

sentences.text: "That's just been created by manufacturers." This video can not be played How sleep-tracking can make your sleep worse Hare says she's noticed trackers causing anxiety among her patients.
sentences.article_title: Why 'sleepmaxxing' could be making your sleep worse

sentences.text: "I've noticed more patients coming to me with data from various trackers, with lots of questions about sleep that... is probably contributing to their sleep difficulties," she says.
sentences.article_title: Why 'sleepmaxxing' could be making your sleep worse

sentences.text: Even though some have had medical tests with reassuring results, this hasn't allayed their fears, she adds.
sentences.article_title: Why 'sleepmaxxing' could be making your sleep worse

sentences.text: "It's great that there's more focus on sleep as part of wellness," she adds.
sentences.article_title: Why 'sleepmaxxing' could be making your sleep worse

sentences.text: "But sleep just does not respond well to attempts to perfect it." One proposed lawsuit against Oura, filed last month in San Francisco, alleges that Oura rings are unable to accurately measure sleep quality and sleep stages, and instead rely on AI-generated estimates that have "a coin flip's chance of being correct".
sentences.article_title: Why 'sleepmaxxing' could be making your sleep worse

sentences.text: In response, Oura told the BBC that it "stand[s] behind our science, research and accuracy claims".
sentences.article_title: Why 'sleepmaxxing' could be making your sleep worse

sentences.text: "We're committed to clearly communicating what Oura measures, what it estimates, and how members should use that information," the company added.
sentences.article_title: Why 'sleepmaxxing' could be making your sleep worse

sentences.text: Studies also show sleep trackers can affect how you function during the day, even if they're not accurate.
sentences.article_title: Why 'sleepmaxxing' could be making your sleep worse

sentences.text: In one study , external from the University of Oxford, participants were given sleep trackers which assigned them a sleep score.
sentences.article_title: Why 'sleepmaxxing' could be making your sleep worse

sentences.text: The scores were randomised, however, and had no relation to how the participants had actually slept.
sentences.article_title: Why 'sleepmaxxing' could be making your sleep worse

sentences.text: The next day participants rated their mood, fatigue levels and alertness, before tests checking their focus and reaction times.
sentences.article_title: Why 'sleepmaxxing' could be making your sleep worse

sentences.text: Researchers found that the people told they'd slept badly reported feeling more fatigued, and were less mentally alert - even though the sleep scores were all fake.
sentences.article_title: Why 'sleepmaxxing' could be making your sleep worse

sentences.text: This is something Jess Hill says she noticed in herself after getting a Garmin watch several years ago.
sentences.article_title: Why 'sleepmaxxing' could be making your sleep worse

sentences.text: "I started to rely on the watch as my Bible for whether I slept well or not," the 32-year-old HR professional from London tells the BBC.
sentences.article_title: Why 'sleepmaxxing' could be making your sleep worse

sentences.text: "I would think, 'I've had awful sleep so I'm going to really struggle today', even if I actually probably had okay sleep.
sentences.article_title: Why 'sleepmaxxing' could be making your sleep worse

sentences.text: "I was awake the other week for four hours in the night, and my watch was like 'wow, great sleep!' - I literally was awake from 01:00 until 05:00," she says.
sentences.article_title: Why 'sleepmaxxing' could be making your sleep worse

sentences.text: The BBC has approached Garmin for comment.
sentences.article_title: Why 'sleepmaxxing' could be making your sleep worse

sentences.text: Jess's sleep scores weren't matching how she actually felt Dr Neil Stanley, sleep expert and author of the book How to Sleep Well, argues that gamifying sleep is creating more disordered sleeping.
sentences.article_title: Why 'sleepmaxxing' could be making your sleep worse

sentences.text: "The thing with tracking your sleep is that it gives you a number, and this means you have a target," he tells the BBC.
sentences.article_title: Why 'sleepmaxxing' could be making your sleep worse

sentences.text: "So you get into this cycle of worrying about your quality of sleep or the quantity of sleep based on figures." He says he carried out research into actigraphy - wrist-worn sleep trackers - around 40 years ago.
sentences.article_title: Why 'sleepmaxxing' could be making your sleep worse

sentences.text: Though commercial trackers now are a bit more sophisticated, they work in much the same way - by measuring your movement - and have the same limitations, he says.
sentences.article_title: Why 'sleepmaxxing' could be making your sleep worse

sentences.text: "If you want to measure sleep, you have to measure the brain," Stanley adds.
sentences.article_title: Why 'sleepmaxxing' could be making your sleep worse

sentences.text: "Unless you're measuring the brain's activities, you're not measuring sleep." Keeping your bedroom cool, dark and quiet - within reason.
sentences.article_title: Why 'sleepmaxxing' could be making your sleep worse

sentences.text: "That doesn't mean it needs to be pitch black, exactly 16C or totally silent," she says.
sentences.article_title: Why 'sleepmaxxing' could be making your sleep worse

sentences.text: "It should be coolish, darkish and quietish." Seeing bright light in the morning, which is good for regulating your circadian rhythm - that is, your body's natural clock.
sentences.article_title: Why 'sleepmaxxing' could be making your sleep worse

sentences.text: Doing light exercise, and eating a "healthy, Mediterranean-style diet with plenty of plant variability".
sentences.article_title: Why 'sleepmaxxing' could be making your sleep worse

sentences.text: Above all, keeping it simple - "anything else, you don't need it".

sentences.text: A million young people are being offered a free meningitis B vaccine.
sentences.article_title: Starting uni? What to know about the free NHS meningitis B jab in England

sentences.text: It comes after concerns over the UK's largest and fastest growing outbreak that happened in Kent earlier this year.
sentences.article_title: Starting uni? What to know about the free NHS meningitis B jab in England

sentences.text: Nearly 90,000 doses of the vaccine have already been given, with 135,000 more booked in for the coming weeks.

sentences.text: So who needs the vaccine, what's in it and where can you get it for free?

sentences.text: The vaccine offers protection against a dangerous strain of meningitis called meningitis B (MenB) that caused the outbreak in Kent.
sentences.article_title: Starting uni? What to know about the free NHS meningitis B jab in England

sentences.text: The vaccine does not contain any live bacteria and cannot cause meningitis.
sentences.article_title: Starting uni? What to know about the free NHS meningitis B jab in England

sentences.text: It is common to get some swelling, redness or tenderness where you have the injection.
sentences.article_title: Starting uni? What to know about the free NHS meningitis B jab in England

sentences.text: You may also get a mild fever, nausea, headache or muscle aches but these symptoms should disappear after one or two days.
sentences.article_title: Starting uni? What to know about the free NHS meningitis B jab in England

sentences.text: More serious side effects are rare.
sentences.article_title: Starting uni? What to know about the free NHS meningitis B jab in England

sentences.article_title: Starting uni? What to know about the free NHS meningitis B jab in England

sentences.article_title: More protein or less? The foods to get you through a heatwave

sentences.text: World Cup footballers aren't the only ones who benefit from hydration breaks: other athletes and pregnant and breastfeeding women are among those who need to drink more.
sentences.article_title: More protein or less? The foods to get you through a heatwave

sentences.article_title: More protein or less? The foods to get you through a heatwave

sentences.article_title: More protein or less? The foods to get you through a heatwave

sentences.article_title: More protein or less? The foods to get you through a heatwave

sentences.article_title: More protein or less? The foods to get you through a heatwave

sentences.text: Experts recommend that those who may be more vulnerable - such as older people and babies and young children - should take extra precautions.
sentences.article_title: What does hot weather do to the body?

sentences.text: As the body gets hotter, blood vessels open up.
sentences.article_title: What does hot weather do to the body?

sentences.text: This lowers your blood pressure and makes your heart work harder to push the blood around the body.
sentences.article_title: What does hot weather do to the body?

sentences.text: This process can cause mild symptoms such as an itchy heat rash or swollen feet.
sentences.article_title: What does hot weather do to the body?

sentences.text: At the same time, sweating leads to the loss of fluids and salt and, crucially, the balance between them in the body changes.
sentences.article_title: What does hot weather do to the body?

sentences.text: This, combined with the lowered blood pressure, can lead to heat exhaustion.

sentences.text: Staying safe in water when the weather's hot Our bodies strive to keep a core temperature of about 37C whether we are in a snowstorm or a heatwave.
sentences.article_title: What does hot weather do to the body?

sentences.text: That is the temperature at which our bodies have evolved to work.
sentences.article_title: What does hot weather do to the body?

sentences.text: But as the weather gets hotter, it is harder for the body to keep its core temperature down.
sentences.article_title: What does hot weather do to the body?

sentences.text: It opens more blood vessels near the skin to lose heat to our surroundings and starts sweating.
sentences.article_title: What does hot weather do to the body?

sentences.text: As the sweat evaporates, it dramatically increases the heat lost from the skin.

sentences.text: If you see someone you think has heat exhaustion , the NHS says you should: , external move them to a cool place get them to lie down and raise their feet slightly get them to drink plenty of water - sports or rehydration drinks are also OK cool their skin - spray or sponge them with cool water and fan them.
sentences.article_title: What does hot weather do to the body?

sentences.text: However, if they do not recover within 30 minutes, then they are at risk of heatstroke .

sentences.text: University applicants in England will be given clearer information about student loans before they take them out, the government has said.
sentences.article_title: Student loan terms to be made clearer in England

sentences.text: Ministers said they would spell out that governments can change repayment rules and that different career choices can affect how much borrowers repay.
sentences.article_title: Student loan terms to be made clearer in England

sentences.text: They agreed to some but not all of the recommendations made by MPs after an inquiry into student loans, and did not say whether they would reverse a freeze to the repayment threshold for some graduates.
sentences.article_title: Student loan terms to be made clearer in England

sentences.text: The inquiry found the way loans had been presented to teenagers amounted to mis-selling , after the BBC revealed the Department for Education (DfE) had compared repayments to £30-a-month phone contracts.
sentences.article_title: Student loan terms to be made clearer in England

sentences.text: The recent debate has centred around Plan 2 loans, which were issued in England between September 2012 and July 2023, and are still issued in Wales.
sentences.article_title: Student loan terms to be made clearer in England

sentences.text: The interest rate on those loans is the Retail Prices Index (RPI) measure of inflation plus up to 3% depending on earnings, and borrowers repay at a rate of 9% of everything they earn over a repayment threshold, which is meant to rise with inflation every year.
sentences.article_title: Student loan terms to be made clearer in England

sentences.text: The loans are written off after 30 years.
sentences.article_title: Student loan terms to be made clearer in England

sentences.text: Campaigners want a lower interest rate, a lower repayment rate and for the government to reverse a decision last year to freeze the threshold at £29,385 for three years in England.
sentences.article_title: Student loan terms to be made clearer in England

sentences.text: Freezing that threshold means graduates start repaying their loans sooner and, once they do, they pay more than they would have done if it had risen with inflation.
sentences.article_title: Student loan terms to be made clearer in England

sentences.text: MPs on the Treasury Committee called for a U-turn on that decision as part of a series of recommendations after an inquiry this summer.
sentences.article_title: Student loan terms to be made clearer in England

sentences.text: It also said "more can be done to help student loan borrowers understand how their loan balance may change over the long term".
sentences.article_title: Student loan terms to be made clearer in England

sentences.text: The government also said giving students long-term predictions of how much they might ultimately repay risked being "misleading" because of "limited" accuracy.
sentences.article_title: Student loan terms to be made clearer in England

sentences.text: It proposed instead to "demonstrate how different life and career choices may affect repayment trajectories", including salary progression, retraining, part-time work, and career breaks.
sentences.article_title: Student loan terms to be made clearer in England

sentences.text: Nick Hillman, director of the Higher Education Policy Institute, who helped design the Plan 2 system, said the government had "absolutely rejected" most of what the Treasury Committee had recommended and its response would not meet the concerns of Plan 2 graduates.
sentences.article_title: Student loan terms to be made clearer in England

sentences.text: Oliver Gardner, founder of the Rethink Repayment campaign, said the government's response "does not go far enough" and he wanted to see "concrete action" in the autumn Budget.
sentences.article_title: Student loan terms to be made clearer in England

sentences.text: While Dame Meg Hillier, chair of the Treasury Committee, said making information clearer was "an important step" but "doesn't help graduates who are angry that they didn't receive the same service and are now facing punitive repayment terms on a loan which keeps growing".
sentences.article_title: Student loan terms to be made clearer in England

sentences.text: She urged the chancellor to reverse the threshold freeze in this autumn's Budget.
sentences.article_title: Student loan terms to be made clearer in England

sentences.text: In March, a BBC investigation found that as well as comparing monthly student loan repayments to phone contracts, the government told presenters to "avoid words [or] phrases like debt" during presentations in schools across England a decade ago.
sentences.article_title: Student loan terms to be made clearer in England

sentences.text: More than 120 MPs and peers recently signed a letter coordinated by the campaign group Rethink Repayment calling for an "urgent review" of the system.
sentences.article_title: Student loan terms to be made clearer in England

sentences.text: One of the signatories, Liberal Democrat MP Tom Gordon, who is a Plan 2 borrower, is set to introduce a bill calling for a review in Parliament next week.
sentences.article_title: Student loan terms to be made clearer in England

sentences.text: Education Secretary Lucy Powell has previously said the interest rate on Plan 2 loans was "egregious" and the issue was at the top of her in-tray.
sentences.article_title: Student loan terms to be made clearer in England

sentences.text: The Student Loans Company said it was working with the government to "provide clear, relatable and trusted guidance".
sentences.article_title: Student loan terms to be made clearer in England

sentences.text: Lucy Shepherd was diagnosed with breast cancer in 2019 A breast cancer survivor says she no longer lives "with the same fear" after a clinical trial enabled her to stop the heart medication she needed following cancer treatment.
sentences.article_title: Heart trial after breast cancer has 'improved my life'

sentences.text: Lucy Shepherd, from Hertfordshire, was diagnosed with triple positive breast cancer shortly after her 33rd birthday, but a routine scan revealed that her heart function had declined during care.
sentences.article_title: Heart trial after breast cancer has 'improved my life'

sentences.text: A new study, described as "hugely encouraging" for patients, has found the majority of breast cancer survivors whose treatment caused heart problems may not need to be on precautionary medication for life.
sentences.article_title: Heart trial after breast cancer has 'improved my life'

sentences.text: "Being part of the trial and having the chance to come off my heart medication has definitely improved my life," Shepherd said.
sentences.article_title: Heart trial after breast cancer has 'improved my life'

sentences.text: The trial - funded by the British Heart Foundation - involved 90 women in their 40s and 50s across four UK hospitals, whose hearts had recovered after a specific type of treatment for breast cancer.
sentences.article_title: Heart trial after breast cancer has 'improved my life'

sentences.text: Most would have been advised to stay on heart drugs for life over concerns heart function would decline if they stopped.
sentences.article_title: Heart trial after breast cancer has 'improved my life'

sentences.text: Researchers found that 98% of patients in the group who stopped taking medication had no change in heart function after one year, with just one woman developing a problem with her heart's pumping ability.
sentences.article_title: Heart trial after breast cancer has 'improved my life'

sentences.text: Women who came off drugs also reported, in questionnaires, a better quality of life.
sentences.article_title: Heart trial after breast cancer has 'improved my life'

sentences.text: Shepherd developed heart problems related to her cancer treatment Shepherd, now 39, said: "Living beyond my cancer treatment was difficult because no one could tell me whether I should stop or continue taking my heart medication.
sentences.article_title: Heart trial after breast cancer has 'improved my life'

sentences.text: "As I got fitter after my cancer treatment ended doctors gradually reduced my heart medication dosages, but I was still having side effects like a low heart rate and fatigue.
sentences.article_title: Heart trial after breast cancer has 'improved my life'

sentences.text: I also had the mental burden of remembering to take them and the worry of what would happen if I missed a dose.
sentences.article_title: Heart trial after breast cancer has 'improved my life'

sentences.text: "I'm still taking hormone therapy, but I don't live with the same fear I once had.
sentences.article_title: Heart trial after breast cancer has 'improved my life'

sentences.text: "Modern breast cancer treatment is a remarkable success story," she said.
sentences.article_title: Heart trial after breast cancer has 'improved my life'

sentences.text: "But the damaging effects of these drugs on the heart leaves survivors and their doctors with difficult questions about ongoing treatment to maintain their heart health.
sentences.article_title: Heart trial after breast cancer has 'improved my life'

sentences.text: "Our study provides the first evidence that heart failure therapies can be safely stopped in survivors whose hearts have recovered, with the support of ongoing close monitoring.
sentences.article_title: Heart trial after breast cancer has 'improved my life'

sentences.text: But the researchers suggest their findings can start important conversations between survivors and their doctors about whether they need to continue treatment long-term.
sentences.article_title: Heart trial after breast cancer has 'improved my life'

sentences.text: Breast cancer is the most common cancer in the UK, with nearly 60,000 new cases diagnosed each year, according to Cancer UK.
sentences.article_title: Heart trial after breast cancer has 'improved my life'

sentences.text: Approximately 15 to 20% of breast cancer cases are HER2-positive, meaning the breast cancer cells have higher than normal levels of a protein called HER2 on their surface.
sentences.article_title: Heart trial after breast cancer has 'improved my life'

sentences.text: In about 10% of cases, this treatment causes problems with heart function.
sentences.article_title: Heart trial after breast cancer has 'improved my life'

sentences.text: Survivors are currently advised to stay on these drugs for life, even after their cancer treatment ends and their heart recovers.
sentences.article_title: Heart trial after breast cancer has 'improved my life'

sentences.text: Dr Sonya Babu-Narayan, clinical director at the British Heart Foundation and consultant cardiologist, said: "These findings will be hugely encouraging for the thousands of breast cancer survivors whose heart health has been affected by lifesaving cancer treatment.
sentences.article_title: Heart trial after breast cancer has 'improved my life'

sentences.text: "The study results give hope that many women will be able to safely stop medicines once their heart has recovered." Do you have a story suggestion for Beds, Herts or Bucks?
